lesson.title: From Spec to Circuit: The Filter Design Process
lesson.summary: Designing a real filter means translating a specification, how sharp the rolloff must be and how much attenuation is needed at a given frequency, into a required filter order, and then choosing between a passive or active topology to realize it.
lesson.body:
So far this chapter has started from a circuit, an RC pair, an RL pair, an RLC triple, or an op-amp stage, and worked out what frequency response it produces. Real filter design usually runs the opposite direction: an engineer starts with a specification, a target cutoff frequency plus some requirement on how much attenuation is needed by a certain frequency past that cutoff, and has to work backward to figure out how complex a circuit is actually required.

The key idea connecting a specification to a circuit is filter order. Each of the single-capacitor or single-inductor filters built earlier in this chapter is a first-order filter, meaning its response rolls off at about 20 dB per decade once you are well past the cutoff frequency. Cascading multiple such stages (with buffering, which is exactly why active filters are so convenient for this) multiplies that steepness: a second-order filter rolls off at about 40 dB per decade, a third-order filter at about 60 dB per decade, and in general an nth-order filter rolls off at roughly 20*n dB per decade, far from the cutoff frequency. Order does not just describe circuit complexity for its own sake, it is a direct, calculable measure of how quickly a filter separates what you want to keep from what you want to reject.

That relationship gives designers a simple sizing tool. Suppose a specification requires at least 60 dB of attenuation by the time you reach a frequency one decade above the cutoff. Since each order contributes about 20 dB of attenuation per decade, the required order is n = 60 / 20 = 3. A third-order filter, three cascaded reactive stages, is the minimum needed to meet that spec; a second-order filter would only reach about 40 dB at that same decade point, falling short. This same reasoning scales to any attenuation and any frequency ratio past cutoff, just replace the one-decade assumption with the actual log10 of the frequency ratio in question.

Order answers "how many stages," but the designer still has to decide how to build each stage: passive or active. A passive RC or RL or RLC stage needs no power, works at very high frequencies, and is cheap and simple, but as the passive filter chapter showed, cascading several passive stages directly runs into the loading problem, each stage's impedance drags on the one before it, distorting the intended response unless the designer carefully accounts for it or adds buffering between stages. An active filter stage, built around an op-amp, buffers itself from its neighbors automatically thanks to its high input and low output impedance, which is precisely why active topologies are so often chosen once a design needs more than one or two cascaded stages, or needs gain in addition to filtering.

Beyond order and topology, real filter design also involves choosing a response shape, families with names like Butterworth, Chebyshev, and Bessel trade off a maximally flat pass band against a sharper rolloff or better preserved signal timing. Those families go beyond what this chapter covers, but the two ideas developed here, order sets how sharp the rolloff is, and passive versus active sets how the stages behave and interact, are the two decisions every filter design starts from.
